lines.text: Six forty-seven A.M. A brand new solar inverter dies on a cold Bengaluru morning. By the end of this course, you'll know exactly why, and how to stop it.
But we start from zero. Electricity in a wire behaves a lot like water in a pipe.
Voltage is the push. Like water pressure, it is how hard the electricity is being pushed. We measure it in volts.
Current is the flow. How much electricity actually moves through the wire every second. We measure it in amps.
Power is push times flow. Volts times amps gives watts. Your turn. Make this panel deliver five hundred and forty watts.
Exactly. Forty-one point six volts times thirteen amps is about five hundred and forty watts. That is the rating printed on a real panel.
One panel pushes about forty-two volts while it works. An inverter wants hundreds. So how do we get there?
Connect panels end to end. That is called series. Each panel adds its push on top of the last one, but the same current flows through all of them.
Predict. Three panels in series. What does the string push?
Volts add up in series. Current stays the same. Like stacking water tanks on top of each other.
Now connect them side by side. That is parallel. The push stays the same, but the flows add up.
Your turn. Build a series string that pushes more than three hundred volts.
Eight panels in series. About three hundred and thirty volts. That is how rooftop strings are built.
Here is the part most new installers get wrong. A panel's voltage is not fixed. It changes with temperature.
Predict. On a freezing morning, does a panel push more volts, fewer volts, or the same?
Let's find out. Drag the thermometer, and watch one panel, and a string of twelve.
Colder means more volts. Below about twenty-two degrees, twelve of these panels push past six hundred volts. The limit of this inverter.
The datasheet gives you the rule. The voltage at twenty-five degrees, and a temperature coefficient. Minus zero point two seven percent, for every degree.
Eight degrees is seventeen degrees colder than twenty-five. Minus times minus is plus. So the voltage rises four point six percent, to fifty-one point nine volts.
Every inverter has a window. Too much voltage, and it is damaged. Too little, and it falls asleep.
This one is damaged above six hundred volts. And it only works between one hundred and twenty, and five hundred and fifty.
So we check two moments. The coldest dawn, when the voltage is highest. And the hottest afternoon, when it is lowest.
Your turn. Pick a number of panels that survives the coldest dawn, and stays awake on the hottest afternoon.
Six hundred divided by fifty-one point nine is eleven point five seven. You can't install half a panel, and you never round up a safety limit. Eleven.
For the minimum, a hot panel works at about thirty-five volts. One twenty divided by thirty-five is three point four. Round up. Four panels, or the inverter sleeps.
Time for a real job ticket. New city, new panel, new inverter. I will guide you step by step.
That is the whole method. Coldest morning for the maximum, round down. Hottest afternoon for the minimum, round up.
Your first project. Mister Sharma wants fourteen panels on his roof. Choose an inverter, design the strings, and explain your design to him.
Solid design. It is saved to your Proof Passport, with every number you chose.
